Trigonometric / hyperbolic definitions
$$\sin z=\frac{e^{iz}-e^{-iz}}{2i},\ \ \cos z=\frac{e^{iz}+e^{-iz}}{2},\ \ \sinh z=\frac{e^z-e^{-z}}2,\ \ \cosh z=\frac{e^z+e^{-z}}2,\ \ \sin iz=i\sinh z,\ \ \cos iz=\cosh z$$
Where: Definitions through e^{iz} and e^{z}.
Use: All identities (sin(iy) = i sinh y, cos(iy) = cosh y) follow from these. Use them to separate real and imaginary parts.
Real & imaginary parts
$$\begin{aligned}\sin(x+iy)&=\sin x\cosh y+i\cos x\sinh y\\ \cos(x+iy)&=\cos x\cosh y-i\sin x\sinh y\\ \sinh(x+iy)&=\sinh x\cos y+i\cosh x\sin y\\ \cosh(x+iy)&=\cosh x\cos y+i\sinh x\sin y\end{aligned}$$
Where: x = Re z, y = Im z.
Use: Expand once and memorise the pattern: trig of x with hyperbolic of y, with i attached to the 'swapped' pair.
Modulus formulas
$$\begin{aligned}&|\sin z|^2=\sin^2x+\sinh^2y\\&|\cos z|^2=\cos^2x+\sinh^2y\\&\cosh^2z-\sinh^2z=1\end{aligned}$$
Where: x = Re z, y = Im z.
Use: Use to show |sin z|² = sin²x + sinh²y, which also proves sin z is unbounded (it can exceed 1 in modulus).
Inverse functions
$$\begin{aligned}&\sin^{-1}z=-i\ln\big(iz+\sqrt{1-z^2}\big)\\&\cos^{-1}z=-i\ln\big(z+i\sqrt{1-z^2}\big)\\&\tan^{-1}z=\frac1{2i}\ln\frac{1+iz}{1-iz}\\&\sinh^{-1}z=\ln\big(z+\sqrt{z^2+1}\big)\end{aligned}$$
Where: Principal branches of the logarithm are used.
Use: Handy for sin⁻¹(cosec θ), tan⁻¹ of complex numbers, and for solving sin z = a. Check the branch of the square root.
Solving sin z = a
$$\sin z=a\ \Rightarrow\ e^{iz}=ia\pm\sqrt{1-a^2}\ \Rightarrow\ z=-i\ln\big(ia\pm\sqrt{1-a^2}\big)+2k\pi$$
Where: a = a given constant, possibly greater than 1.
Use: Put w = e^{iz}: w − 1/w = 2ia → quadratic in w. Take logs, then add all 2kπ solutions.
Note: For sin z = cosh 4 (> 1): z = π/2 + 2kπ ± 4i.
Real quadratic factors of z⁴ + a⁴
$$z^4+4=(z^2+2z+2)(z^2-2z+2)$$
Where: Complex roots of a real polynomial occur in conjugate pairs.
Use: Pair each root with its conjugate: (z−a)(z−ā) = z² − 2Re(a)z + |a|², a real quadratic factor.
Note: Roots: ±1 ± i. General: z⁴+4a⁴ = (z²+2az+2a²)(z²−2az+2a²).
Conjugate & division rules
$$\begin{aligned}&\overline{z_1\pm z_2}=\bar z_1\pm\bar z_2\\&\overline{z_1z_2}=\bar z_1\bar z_2\\&\overline{\Big(\frac{z_1}{z_2}\Big)}=\frac{\bar z_1}{\bar z_2}\\&\frac1z=\frac{\bar z}{|z|^2}\end{aligned}$$
Where: z̄ = complex conjugate.
Use: Divide complex numbers by multiplying numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator.
Roots of unity & Euler's formula

Euler's Formula & $n$-th Roots of Unity: The $n$ roots of $z^n = 1$ are $1, \omega, \omega^2, \dots, \omega^{n-1}$ where $\omega = e^{2\pi i/n}$, forming a regular $n$-gon on the unit circle whose sum is zero:

$$\begin{aligned}&\omega=e^{2\pi i/n},\ \ 1+\omega+\omega^2+\cdots+\omega^{n-1}=0\\&e^{i\theta}=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta,\ \ e^{i\pi}+1=0\end{aligned}$$
Where: ω = primitive nth root of unity.
Use: Sum of all nth roots of any number is zero; used in polynomial and series problems.
Analytic functions, Cauchy–Riemann, harmonic functionsFreq: 5/50/11
Derivative of f(z)
$$\begin{aligned}&f'(z)=\lim_{\Delta z\to0}\frac{f(z+\Delta z)-f(z)}{\Delta z}\\&(\text{must be independent of direction})\end{aligned}$$
Where: Δz → 0 along every possible direction in the plane.
Use: The limit must be the same for all directions; this is why z̄ and |z|² fail. It leads directly to the C–R equations.
Cauchy–Riemann equations

Cauchy–Riemann Equations (Cartesian Form): Necessary condition for $f(z) = u(x,y) + i v(x,y)$ to be differentiable at $z = x+iy$:

$$\begin{aligned}&u_x=v_y\\&u_y=-v_x\\&f'(z)=u_x+iv_x=v_y-iu_y\end{aligned}$$
Where: u = Re f, v = Im f, partials taken with respect to x, y.
Use: Necessary for differentiability; with continuous partials they are also sufficient. Then f′ = ux + i vx.
Derivation outline
  1. Take $\Delta z=\Delta x$ (real): $f'=u_x+iv_x$.
  2. Take $\Delta z=i\Delta y$: $f'=\dfrac{1}{i}(u_y+iv_y)=v_y-iu_y$.
  3. The two limits must be equal (differentiability).
  4. Equate real and imaginary parts: $u_x=v_y$ and $u_y=-v_x$.
C–R in polar form

Cauchy–Riemann Equations (Polar Form): For $f(re^{i\theta}) = u(r,\theta) + i v(r,\theta)$ at $r > 0$:

$$\begin{aligned}&u_r=\frac1rv_\theta\\&v_r=-\frac1ru_\theta\\&f'(z)=e^{-i\theta}(u_r+iv_r)\end{aligned}$$
Where: (r, θ) polar coordinates; ur = ∂u/∂r, v_θ = ∂v/∂θ.
Use: Use when f is given as a function of r and θ (e.g. (1/r⁴)cos4θ − i(1/r⁴)sin4θ). Do not forget the factor 1/r.
Derivation outline
  1. Use $x=r\cos\theta$, $y=r\sin\theta$ and the chain rule: $u_r=u_x\cos\theta+u_y\sin\theta$, $u_\theta=-ru_x\sin\theta+ru_y\cos\theta$.
  2. Same for $v$.
  3. Substitute $u_x=v_y$, $u_y=-v_x$ and simplify.
  4. $u_r=\dfrac1rv_\theta$, $v_r=-\dfrac1ru_\theta$.
C–R in complex form
$$\frac{\partial f}{\partial\bar z}=0\iff f\text{ analytic}$$
Where: ∂/∂z̄ = ½(∂/∂x + i∂/∂y).
Use: Quick test: if f contains z̄ (or |z|) in any essential way, ∂f/∂z̄ ≠ 0 and f is not analytic.
Note: Any occurrence of z̄ (or |z|) that cannot be removed means f is not analytic; e.g. |z|² is differentiable only at z = 0.
Necessary & sufficient condition

Necessary & Sufficient Condition for Analyticity: $f(z) = u(x,y) + i v(x,y)$ is analytic in a domain $D$ if and only if $u_x, u_y, v_x, v_y$ exist, are continuous, and satisfy the C–R equations throughout $D$:

$$u,v\ \text{have continuous first partials and satisfy C–R in a domain}\iff f=u+iv\ \text{is analytic there}$$
Where: D = open connected region of the plane.
Use: Analytic in D means differentiable at every point of D (a neighbourhood), not just at one point.
Harmonic function

Harmonic Function Definition & Theorem: If $f(z) = u(x,y) + i v(x,y)$ is analytic in $D$, then both $u$ and $v$ satisfy Laplace's 2D equation in $D$:

$$\begin{aligned}&\nabla^2u=u_{xx}+u_{yy}=0\\&\nabla^2v=0\end{aligned}$$
Where: uxx, uyy = second partials.
Use: u, v being the real and imaginary parts of an analytic function makes both harmonic. Check Laplace's equation to show a given function is harmonic.
Harmonic conjugate

Harmonic Conjugate Construction: Given a harmonic function $u(x,y)$, its harmonic conjugate $v(x,y)$ such that $f(z)=u+iv$ is analytic is obtained from the exact differential $dv = -u_y\,dx + u_x\,dy$:

$$dv=-u_y\,dx+u_x\,dy\ \Rightarrow\ v=\int(-u_y)\,dx+\int\big(\text{terms of }u_x\text{ free of }x\big)\,dy$$
Where: v is the harmonic conjugate of u; vx = −uy, vy = ux.
Use: Integrate one C–R equation, then fix the unknown function of the other variable from the second equation. Constant of integration is arbitrary.
Milne–Thomson method

Milne–Thomson Method: Directly constructs an analytic function $f(z) = u + iv$ from its real part $u(x,y)$ or imaginary part $v(x,y)$ without finding the conjugate first:

$$\begin{aligned}&\text{given }u:\ f(z)=\int\big[u_x(z,0)-i\,u_y(z,0)\big]dz+C\\&\text{given }v:\ f(z)=\int\big[v_y(z,0)+i\,v_x(z,0)\big]dz+C\end{aligned}$$
Where: Set y = 0 and replace x by z in the partial derivatives.
Use: Fast way to build f(z) when only u or v is known. The final expression involves z only; fix the constant from a given value.
Orthogonal trajectories

Orthogonal Trajectories Theorem: For any analytic function $f(z) = u(x,y) + i v(x,y)$, the level curves $u(x,y) = c_1$ and $v(x,y) = c_2$ intersect at right angles wherever $f'(z) \neq 0$:

$$\begin{aligned}&\text{family }u(x,y)=c\ \Rightarrow\ \text{trajectories }v(x,y)=c'\ \ (v=\text{harmonic conjugate})\\&\nabla u\cdot\nabla v=0\end{aligned}$$
Where: Curves u(x,y) = c and v(x,y) = c′ cut each other at 90°.
Use: To find trajectories of a family, take the family as u = const, find the conjugate v, and the orthogonal family is v = const.
Test of analyticity: standard results
$$\begin{aligned}&e^z,\ \sin z,\ \cos z,\ z^n\ \text{entire}\\&\bar z,\ |z|,\ \operatorname{Re}z,\ \operatorname{Im}z\ \text{nowhere analytic}\\&e^{z^2}\ \text{entire}\end{aligned}$$
Where: 'Entire' = analytic on the whole plane.
Use: e^z, sin z, cos z, polynomials are entire; z̄, |z|, Re z, Im z are nowhere analytic.
Derivative rules & polar Laplacian
$$\begin{aligned}&\frac{d}{dz}z^n=nz^{n-1},\ \ \frac{d}{dz}e^z=e^z,\ \ \frac{d}{dz}\sin z=\cos z,\ \ \frac{d}{dz}\ln z=\frac1z\\&\nabla^2u=u_{rr}+\frac1ru_r+\frac1{r^2}u_{\theta\theta}\end{aligned}$$
Where: Ordinary rules hold for analytic functions; the polar Laplacian is used in harmonic-function problems.
Use: Differentiate with the usual product/chain rules; verify polar harmonicity with the Laplacian.
Complex integration, Cauchy's theorem, ML inequalityFreq: 5/50/10
Contour integral
$$\int_Cf(z)\,dz=\int_a^bf(z(t))\,z'(t)\,dt=\int_C(u+iv)(dx+i\,dy)$$
Where: C = path, z(t) = parametrisation for a ≤ t ≤ b, z′ = dz/dt.
Use: Parametrise, substitute, integrate in t. For closed paths use the theorems instead whenever possible.
Standard parametrisations
$$\begin{aligned}&\text{segment }z_1\to z_2:\ z=z_1+t(z_2-z_1),\ 0\le t\le1\\&\text{circle: }z=a+Re^{i\theta},\ dz=iRe^{i\theta}d\theta\\&y=mx:\ z=(1+im)x\end{aligned}$$
Where: a = centre, R = radius, θ from 0 to 2π for a full circle.
Use: Counter-clockwise = θ increasing. A segment is z₁ + t(z₂ − z₁), 0 ≤ t ≤ 1. Line y = mx: z = (1+im)x.
ML-inequality

ML-Estimation Inequality (Darboux Bounding Theorem): If $|f(z)| \le M$ at every point on a contour $C$ of finite length $L$, then:

$$\begin{aligned}&\Big|\int_Cf(z)\,dz\Big|\le ML\\&M=\max_{C}|f(z)|,\quad L=\text{length of }C\end{aligned}$$
Where: M = maximum of |f| on C, L = length of C.
Use: Overestimate |f| using the largest numerator and the smallest denominator bound (reverse triangle inequality), and use exact arc length.
Derivation outline
  1. $\left|\int_Cf\,dz\right|\le\int_C|f||dz|$ (modulus of an integral ≤ integral of the modulus).
  2. On $C$: $|f|\le M$.
  3. $\int_C|dz|=L$ (arc length).
  4. So $\left|\int_Cf\,dz\right|\le ML$.
Useful bounds on C
$$\begin{aligned}&|z^2-1|\ge|z|^2-1\\&|z^2+z+1|\ge|z|^2-|z|-1\\&|e^{iz}|=e^{-y}\le1\ (y\ge0)\\&|e^{z}|=e^{x}\end{aligned}$$
Where: z lies on the contour, |z| = R or similar.
Use: Lower bounds on denominators: |z² − 1| ≥ |z|² − 1. On the upper half plane |e^{iz}| = e^{−y} ≤ 1.
Cauchy–Goursat theorem

Cauchy–Goursat Theorem: If $f(z)$ is analytic at all points interior to and on a simple closed contour $C$, then $\oint_C f(z)\,dz = 0$.

$$\oint_Cf(z)\,dz=0\quad(f\text{ analytic inside and on }C)$$
Where: f analytic inside and on the simple closed contour C.
Use: The integral is zero. If there is a singularity inside, use the residue theorem or Cauchy's formula instead.
Cauchy integral formula

Cauchy's Integral Formula: If $f(z)$ is analytic everywhere inside and on a positively oriented simple closed contour $C$ and $a$ lies strictly inside $C$, then:

$$f(a)=\frac1{2\pi i}\oint_C\frac{f(z)}{z-a}\,dz\quad(a\text{ inside }C)$$
Where: a lies strictly inside C, f analytic inside and on C.
Use: Rewrite the integrand as f(z)/(z − a); the integral equals 2πi f(a). With several poles, partial fractions or small circles.
Derivation outline
  1. Write $\dfrac{f(z)}{z-a}=\dfrac{f(a)}{z-a}+\dfrac{f(z)-f(a)}{z-a}$.
  2. Deform $C$ to a small circle $|z-a|=\varepsilon$ (Cauchy's theorem).
  3. First term: $\oint\dfrac{dz}{z-a}=2\pi i$, so it gives $2\pi if(a)$.
  4. Second term: bounded by $\max|f(z)-f(a)|\cdot2\pi\to0$ as $\varepsilon\to0$ (continuity), so $f(a)=\dfrac{1}{2\pi i}\oint\dfrac{f(z)}{z-a}dz$.
Derivatives of an analytic function

Generalized Cauchy Integral Formula for Derivatives: An analytic function $f(z)$ inside $C$ possesses derivatives of all orders at every interior point $a$:

$$\begin{aligned}&f^{(n)}(a)=\frac{n!}{2\pi i}\oint_C\frac{f(z)}{(z-a)^{n+1}}\,dz\\&\oint_C\frac{f(z)}{(z-a)^{n+1}}dz=\frac{2\pi i}{n!}f^{(n)}(a)\end{aligned}$$
Where: n! / (2πi) factor; f⁽ⁿ⁾(a) = n-th derivative at a.
Use: Use for a pole of order n+1 of the form f(z)/(z−a)ⁿ⁺¹ with f analytic (e.g. e^{3z}/(z−i)⁴).
Fundamental integral
$$\oint_{|z-a|=r}\frac{dz}{(z-a)^n}=\begin{cases}2\pi i&n=1\\0&n\ne1\end{cases}$$
Where: a = point inside the circle |z − a| = r.
Use: Only the 1/(z−a) term contributes 2πi; every other integer power integrates to zero.
Path independence

Fundamental Theorem of Complex Contour Integration (Path Independence): If $f(z)$ is analytic in a simply connected domain $D$ with antiderivative $F'(z) = f(z)$, then:

$$\int_{z_1}^{z_2}f\,dz=F(z_2)-F(z_1)\quad(f\ \text{analytic},\ F'=f)$$
Where: F′ = f; z₁, z₂ = end points.
Use: Valid only when f is analytic on a simply connected region containing the path. For z̄ or |z|² the answer depends on the path.
Note: For non-analytic integrands such as z̄ or (z̄)² the value depends on the path: parametrise each path separately.
Multiply-connected regions

Principle of Deformation of Contours (Multiply-Connected Domain): If $f(z)$ is analytic between outer contour $C$ and interior contours $C_1, \dots, C_n$ (all oriented counterclockwise), then:

$$\begin{aligned}&\oint_{C}f\,dz=\sum_k\oint_{C_k}f\,dz\\&(C_k\ \text{small circles around the singularities inside }C)\end{aligned}$$
Where: Ck = small circles around each excluded singularity.
Use: Deform the contour to the sum of small circles; each circle contributes via Cauchy's formula or a residue.
Consequences of Cauchy's theoremFreq: 3/50/4
Gauss mean value property

Gauss's Mean Value Theorem for Analytic Functions: If $f(z)$ is analytic inside and on the circle $|z-a|=r$, its value at the centre $a$ equals the arithmetic mean of its values on the circumference:

$$f(a)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}f\big(a+re^{i\theta}\big)\,d\theta$$
Where: f analytic in and on the circle |z−a| = r.
Use: The value at the centre equals the average on the circle.
Cauchy's inequality

Cauchy's Inequality: If $f(z)$ is analytic inside and on the circle $|z-a|=r$ and $|f(z)|\le M$ on that circle, then the $n$-th derivative at the centre satisfies:

$$|f^{(n)}(a)|\le\frac{n!\,M}{r^n}$$
Where: M = max|f| on |z−a| = r.
Use: Follows from the ML-inequality; used to prove Liouville's theorem.
Liouville & maximum modulus
  • Liouville: a bounded entire function is constant.
  • Maximum modulus: a non-constant analytic f cannot attain its maximum of |f| in the interior of the region.
  • Fundamental theorem of algebra: every non-constant polynomial has a root in ℂ.
$|f(z)|\le M\ (\forall z\in\mathbb{C})\implies f(z)=\text{const};\qquad \max_{z\in\overline{D}}|f(z)|=\max_{z\in\partial D}|f(z)|$
Where: Liouville requires f(z) to be entire (analytic on all of ℂ) and bounded; Maximum Modulus applies on a bounded domain D.
Use: Proves the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra: if P(z) ≠ 0 on ℂ, then 1/P(z) is bounded and entire, hence constant.
Morera's theorem

If f is continuous on a domain and ∮C f dz = 0 for every closed triangle/contour in it, then f is analytic.

$f\in C(D)\text{ and }\oint_C f(z)\,dz=0\ (\forall\text{ closed }C\subset D)\implies f(z)\text{ is analytic in }D$
Where: D = open connected domain in ℂ; f assumed continuous on D.
Use: Converse of Cauchy's integral theorem; used to prove analyticity of uniform limits and integral-defined functions.
Taylor & Laurent series, singularities, residuesFreq: 5/50/12
Taylor series (complex)

Taylor's Theorem for Analytic Functions: If $f(z)$ is analytic inside the open disk $|z-a| < R$, it converges uniquely to the power series:

$$\begin{aligned}&f(z)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n(z-a)^n\\&a_n=\frac{f^{(n)}(a)}{n!}=\frac1{2\pi i}\oint\frac{f(z)}{(z-a)^{n+1}}dz\\&R=\text{distance from }a\text{ to the nearest singularity}\end{aligned}$$
Where: a = centre; R = radius of convergence.
Use: R equals the distance from a to the nearest singularity of f; the series converges in that disc.
Laurent series

Laurent's Expansion Theorem: If $f(z)$ is analytic throughout the annular ring $R_1 < |z-a| < R_2$, it has the unique two-sided expansion:

$$\begin{aligned}&f(z)=\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}a_n(z-a)^n=\underbrace{\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n(z-a)^n}_{\text{analytic part}}+\underbrace{\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{a_{-n}}{(z-a)^n}}_{\text{principal part}}\\&a_n=\frac1{2\pi i}\oint\frac{f(z)}{(z-a)^{n+1}}dz\end{aligned}$$
Where: an = coefficients (n may be negative); the n < 0 part is the principal part.
Use: Valid in an annulus. Different annuli give different Laurent series for the same function. a₋₁ is the residue.
Derivation outline
  1. Take the annulus $r_1<|z-a|<r_2$ with boundary circles $C_1$ (outer) and $C_2$ (inner).
  2. Cauchy's formula for the annulus: $f(z)=\dfrac1{2\pi i}\oint_{C_1}\dfrac{f(w)}{w-z}dw-\dfrac1{2\pi i}\oint_{C_2}\dfrac{f(w)}{w-z}dw$.
  3. Expand $\dfrac1{w-z}$ in powers of $(z-a)/(w-a)$ on $C_1$ and of $(w-a)/(z-a)$ on $C_2$ (geometric series).
  4. Collect terms: $f(z)=\sum_{n=-\infty}^\infty a_n(z-a)^n$ with $a_n=\dfrac1{2\pi i}\oint\dfrac{f(w)}{(w-a)^{n+1}}dw$.
Geometric-series expansions
$$\begin{aligned}&\frac1{1-w}=\sum_{n=0}^\infty w^n\ (|w|<1)\\&\frac1{1-w}=-\sum_{n=1}^\infty w^{-n}\ (|w|>1)\\&\frac1{z-a}=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{a^n}{z^{n+1}}\ (|z|>|a|)\end{aligned}$$
Where: w = the expression in z that is small in the given region.
Use: For |z| > |a| write 1/(z − a) = (1/z)·1/(1 − a/z); for |z − c| small use powers of (z − c). Always split into partial fractions first.
Note: Rule: for the region |z−c| < r use powers of (z−c)/…; for |z| > R use powers of 1/z. Always split with partial fractions first.
Standard Laurent pieces
$$\begin{aligned}&e^{1/z}=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac1{n!z^n}\\&\frac{\sin z}{z}=1-\frac{z^2}{3!}+\cdots\\&\frac1{z-2}=\frac{1}{(z-1)-1}\ \ (\text{expand in }w=z-1)\end{aligned}$$
Where: e^{1/z}, sin z / z, shifts z − 1 etc.
Use: Substituting into known Maclaurin series is much faster than computing coefficients by integrals.
Classification of isolated singularities

Classification of Isolated Singularities: An isolated singularity $z=a$ is classified by the principal (negative-power) part of its Laurent expansion:

$$\begin{aligned}&\text{removable: no principal part,}\quad \text{pole of order }m:\ a_{-m}\neq0,\ a_{-n}=0\ (n>m)\\&\text{essential: infinitely many negative powers (e.g. }e^{1/z}\text{ at }0)\end{aligned}$$
Where: Isolated singularity at a.
Use: Look at the principal part: none ⇒ removable; finitely many terms ⇒ pole of that order; infinitely many ⇒ essential.
Residue
$$\operatorname{Res}_{z=a}f=a_{-1}=\frac1{2\pi i}\oint f\,dz$$
Where: a₋₁ = coefficient of 1/(z − a) in the Laurent series.
Use: The residue is the only part that survives in ∮f dz = 2πi·a₋₁.
Simple pole
$$\begin{aligned}&\operatorname{Res}_{z=a}f=\lim_{z\to a}(z-a)f(z)\\&f=\frac{p}{q}:\ \ \operatorname{Res}=\frac{p(a)}{q'(a)}\end{aligned}$$
Where: p/q with q(a) = 0 and q′(a) ≠ 0.
Use: Fastest for ratios such as 1/(z²+1) or e^z/sin z. Residue = p(a)/q′(a).
Pole of order m
$$\operatorname{Res}_{z=a}f=\frac1{(m-1)!}\lim_{z\to a}\frac{d^{m-1}}{dz^{m-1}}\Big[(z-a)^mf(z)\Big]$$
Where: m = order of the pole.
Use: Multiply by (z−a)^m, differentiate m−1 times, take the limit, divide by (m−1)!. Do the algebra before differentiating.
Residue theorem

Cauchy's Residue Theorem: If $f(z)$ is analytic inside and on a positively oriented simple closed contour $C$ except for isolated singularities $a_1, \dots, a_m$ inside $C$, then:

$$\begin{aligned}&\oint_Cf(z)\,dz=2\pi i\sum_{k}\operatorname{Res}_{z=a_k}f\\&(\text{poles }a_k\text{ INSIDE }C\text{ only})\end{aligned}$$
Where: ak = poles inside C; sum over those only.
Use: First decide which poles lie inside the given contour (circle or ellipse), then add their residues and multiply by 2πi.
Note: First decide which poles lie inside the given contour: |z| = 2.5 contains z = 1, 2 but not 3; |z+2|+|z−2| = 6 is an ellipse with foci ±2 and semi-axes 3 and √5.
Derivation outline
  1. Surround each pole $a_k$ by a small circle $C_k$ inside $C$.
  2. Cauchy's theorem for the multiply-connected region: $\oint_C f\,dz=\sum_k\oint_{C_k}f\,dz$.
  3. On each small circle only the $\dfrac{a_{-1}}{z-a_k}$ term contributes: $\oint_{C_k}f\,dz=2\pi i\,a_{-1}$.
  4. Therefore $\oint_Cf\,dz=2\pi i\sum\operatorname{Res}$.
Residue at ∞ / sum
$$\sum\text{(all residues incl. }\infty)=0;\quad \operatorname{Res}_{z=\infty}f(z)=-\operatorname{Res}_{w=0}\!\left[\frac{1}{w^2}f\!\left(\frac{1}{w}\right)\right]=-\frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_C f(z)\,dz$$
Where: All finite residues plus the residue at infinity sum to zero.
Use: A useful check, or a shortcut when a contour encloses many poles.
Radius of convergence tests
$$\begin{aligned}&R=\lim_{n\to\infty}\Big|\frac{a_n}{a_{n+1}}\Big|\\&\frac1R=\limsup_{n\to\infty}|a_n|^{1/n}\end{aligned}$$
Where: an = coefficients of Σ an (z−a)ⁿ.
Use: Ratio test is usually quickest; the series converges for |z − a| < R.
Residues of standard functions
$$\begin{aligned}&\operatorname{Res}_{z=ia}\frac{1}{z^2+a^2}=\frac{1}{2ia},\quad \operatorname{Res}_{z=n\pi}\cot z=1,\quad \operatorname{Res}_{z=n\pi}\csc z=(-1)^n\\&\operatorname{Res}_{z=0}\frac{e^z}{z^n}=\frac1{(n-1)!},\quad \operatorname{Res}_{z=0}e^{1/z}=1,\quad \operatorname{Res}_{z=a}\frac{\phi(z)}{(z-a)^m}=\frac{\phi^{(m-1)}(a)}{(m-1)!}\end{aligned}$$
Where: a > 0, n integer.
Use: Use directly instead of re-deriving; coth z and cot z have poles at iπn and nπ respectively.
Real integrals by contour integrationFreq: 4/50/7
Trigonometric integrals
$$\begin{aligned}&\int_0^{2\pi}F(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)\,d\theta=\oint_{|z|=1}F\Big(\frac{z+z^{-1}}{2},\frac{z-z^{-1}}{2i}\Big)\frac{dz}{iz}\\&\cos n\theta=\operatorname{Re}\,z^n\end{aligned}$$
Where: z = e^{iθ} traces |z| = 1; dθ = dz/(iz).
Use: Replace cos θ, sin θ by (z ± 1/z)/2, (z − 1/z)/2i; integrate around the unit circle with residues inside it.
Derivation outline
  1. Let $z=e^{i\theta}$ (unit circle): $d\theta=\dfrac{dz}{iz}$.
  2. $\cos\theta=\dfrac{z+z^{-1}}2$, $\sin\theta=\dfrac{z-z^{-1}}{2i}$.
  3. The integral becomes $\oint_{|z|=1}R(z)\,dz$ with $R$ rational.
  4. Evaluate with the residue theorem using poles inside the unit circle.
Shortcut: 1/(a + b cos θ)
$$\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{d\theta}{a+b\cos\theta}=\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{a^2-b^2}}\quad(a>|b|)$$
Where: a > |b| ensures no real singularity.
Use: Gives the answer 2π/√(a² − b²) with no residue calculation.
Shortcut: cos nθ / (1 − 2p cos θ + p²)
$$\begin{aligned}&\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{\cos n\theta}{1-2p\cos\theta+p^2}\,d\theta=\frac{2\pi p^n}{1-p^2}\\&(0<p<1)\end{aligned}$$
Where: 0 < p < 1; n integer.
Use: Rewrite the denominator as k(1 − 2p cos θ + p²), then multiply by 1/k. Example: 5 − 4cos θ = 4(1 − cos θ + 1/4) with p = ½.
Note: ∫₀^{2π} cos3θ /(5−4cosθ) dθ: 5−4cosθ = 4(1−2p cosθ+p²) with p = ½ ⇒ π/12.
Rational functions over ℝ
$$\begin{aligned}&\int_{-\infty}^\infty\frac{P(x)}{Q(x)}dx=2\pi i\sum_{\operatorname{Im}a_k>0}\operatorname{Res}\\&(\deg Q\ge\deg P+2,\ Q\ne0\text{ on }\mathbb R)\end{aligned}$$
Where: deg Q ≥ deg P + 2 so the big arc vanishes.
Use: Close the contour with a large semicircle in the upper half plane and add residues at poles with Im > 0.
Fourier-type (Jordan)
$$\begin{aligned}&\int_{-\infty}^\infty f(x)e^{iax}dx=2\pi i\sum_{\operatorname{Im}z_k>0}\operatorname{Res}\big[f(z)e^{iaz}\big]\\&a>0\end{aligned}$$
Where: a > 0; f decays at infinity.
Use: Jordan's lemma lets you ignore the arc when f → 0. Close in the upper half plane for e^{iax}, a > 0.
Big-semicircle estimate
$$\Big|\int_{C_R}f\,dz\Big|\le\pi R\max_{C_R}|f|\ \to0\quad\text{if }|f|=O(R^{-2})$$
Where: CR = semicircle of radius R.
Use: Use the ML-inequality to show the arc integral → 0 as R → ∞.
Standard definite integrals
$$\begin{aligned}&\int_{-\infty}^\infty\frac{dx}{x^2+a^2}=\frac\pi a\\&\int_0^\infty\frac{\cos mx}{x^2+a^2}dx=\frac{\pi}{2a}e^{-ma}\\&\int_{-\infty}^\infty\frac{dx}{(x^2+a^2)^2}=\frac{\pi}{2a^3}\\&\int_0^\infty\frac{\sin x}{x}dx=\frac\pi2\end{aligned}$$
Where: a > 0, m > 0.
Use: Checks for contour-integration answers; each follows from the residue theorem with a semicircle.
Bilinear (Möbius) transformationFreq: 2/50/5
Definition
$$\begin{aligned}&w=\frac{az+b}{cz+d}\\&ad-bc\neq0\\&z=\frac{dw-b}{-cw+a}\end{aligned}$$
Where: a, b, c, d complex constants.
Use: Maps the extended plane one-to-one; the condition ad − bc ≠ 0 excludes degenerate constant maps.
Three-point (cross-ratio) formula
$$\frac{(w-w_1)(w_2-w_3)}{(w-w_3)(w_2-w_1)}=\frac{(z-z_1)(z_2-z_3)}{(z-z_3)(z_2-z_1)}$$
Where: Three points z₁, z₂, z₃ map to w₁, w₂, w₃.
Use: Cross-ratios are preserved: equate the two cross-ratios and solve for w in terms of z.
Properties
$$\begin{aligned}&\text{circles / lines}\mapsto\text{circles / lines}\\&\text{conformal}\\&\text{fixed points: }z=\frac{az+b}{cz+d}\\&w=\frac1z:\ |z|=r\mapsto|w|=\frac1r\end{aligned}$$
Where: Circles and lines map to circles or lines.
Use: To find the image of a region, map the boundary and test one interior point; |z| = r under w = 1/z gives |w| = 1/r.
Image of a region
  1. Invert the map to get z in terms of w.
  2. Substitute into the boundary (|z| = r, |z| < 1 …).
  3. Simplify to a circle/line in w and test one interior point.
$z=\frac{dw-b}{-cw+a};\qquad |z|=R\implies \left|\frac{dw-b}{cw-a}\right|=R$
Where: w = (az+b)/(cz+d) with ad − bc ≠ 0.
Use: Substitute z(w) into the boundary equation (e.g. |z| = 1 or z + z̄ = 0) and test z = 0 to see which side is the image.
Special Möbius maps
$$\begin{aligned}&w=z+b\ (\text{translation}),\ \ w=e^{i\alpha}z\ (\text{rotation}),\ \ w=az\ (\text{magnification}),\ \ w=\frac1z\ (\text{inversion})\\&w=\frac{z-i}{z+i}:\ \text{upper half-plane}\to|w|<1\end{aligned}$$
Where: Compose these four basic maps to build any bilinear map.
Use: Unit disc onto itself: w = e^{iα}(z − a)/(1 − āz), |a| < 1.
Vector algebra, lines, planes, linear dependenceFreq: 5/50/7
Dot & cross product, projection
$$\begin{aligned}&\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\cos\theta,\qquad |\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}|=|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\sin\theta\\&\text{comp}_{\mathbf{b}}\mathbf{a}=\frac{\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}}{|\mathbf{b}|},\qquad \text{proj}_{\mathbf{b}}\mathbf{a}=\frac{\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}}{|\mathbf{b}|^2}\mathbf{b}\end{aligned}$$
Where: θ = angle between a and b (0 ≤ θ ≤ π).
Use: a · b = 0 tests perpendicularity; a × b = 0 tests collinearity; |a × b| = area of parallelogram, ½|a × b| = area of triangle.
Scalar triple product (box product)
$$[\mathbf{a}\ \mathbf{b}\ \mathbf{c}]=\mathbf{a}\cdot(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c})=\begin{vmatrix}a_1&a_2&a_3\\b_1&b_2&b_3\\c_1&c_2&c_3\end{vmatrix},\qquad V_{\text{tetra}}=\frac16|[\mathbf{a}\ \mathbf{b}\ \mathbf{c}]|$$
Where: a, b, c = three edges from a common vertex.
Use: |[a b c]| = volume of parallelepiped. Three vectors are coplanar iff [a b c] = 0. Cyclic permutations keep the sign.
Vector triple product & Lagrange identity
$$\begin{aligned}&\mathbf{a}\times(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c})=(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{c})\mathbf{b}-(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b})\mathbf{c}\\&(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b})\cdot(\mathbf{c}\times\mathbf{d})=(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{c})(\mathbf{b}\cdot\mathbf{d})-(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{d})(\mathbf{b}\cdot\mathbf{c})\end{aligned}$$
Where: BAC−CAB rule; parentheses matter because cross product is not associative.
Use: For quadruple cross product (a × b) × (c × d), treat u = a × b as a single vector: [a b d]c − [a b c]d.
Reciprocal system of vectors
$$\mathbf{a}'=\frac{\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c}}{[\mathbf{a}\ \mathbf{b}\ \mathbf{c}]},\qquad \mathbf{b}'=\frac{\mathbf{c}\times\mathbf{a}}{[\mathbf{a}\ \mathbf{b}\ \mathbf{c}]},\qquad \mathbf{c}'=\frac{\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}}{[\mathbf{a}\ \mathbf{b}\ \mathbf{c}]},\qquad [\mathbf{a}'\ \mathbf{b}'\ \mathbf{c}']=\frac{1}{[\mathbf{a}\ \mathbf{b}\ \mathbf{c}]}$$
Where: [a b c] ≠ 0 (non-coplanar basis).
Use: Satisfies a · a' = b · b' = c · c' = 1 and dot product of unlike pairs = 0; any vector r = (r·a')a + (r·b')b + (r·c')c.
Linear dependence & independence
$$c_1\mathbf{v}_1+c_2\mathbf{v}_2+\cdots+c_k\mathbf{v}_k=\mathbf{0};\quad [\vec{AB}\ \vec{AC}\ \vec{AD}]=0\ (\text{4 points coplanar});\quad k\mathbf{r}+\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{b}\implies \mathbf{r}=\frac{k^2\mathbf{b}+(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b})\mathbf{a}-k(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b})}{k(k^2+|\mathbf{a}|^2)}$$
Where: c_i = scalars.
Use: Only trivial solution c_i = 0 ⇒ linearly independent. In R³, 3 vectors are linearly dependent iff their determinant [v₁ v₂ v₃] = 0 (coplanar).
Equations of lines & planes in 3-D
$$\text{Line: }\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{r}_0+t\mathbf{v};\qquad \text{Plane: }(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}_0)\cdot\mathbf{n}=0\iff ax+by+cz=d$$
Where: r₀ = point on line/plane, v = direction vector, n = normal vector = (r₁ − r₀) × (r₂ − r₀).
Use: Distance from point P to plane: |PM · n|/|n|. Distance from point P to line: |(P − r₀) × v|/|v|.
Shortest distance between skew lines
$$d=\frac{|(\mathbf{r}_2-\mathbf{r}_1)\cdot(\mathbf{v}_1\times\mathbf{v}_2)|}{|\mathbf{v}_1\times\mathbf{v}_2|}$$
Where: Lines r = r₁ + t v₁ and r = r₂ + s v₂.
Use: The lines intersect (are coplanar) iff (r₂ − r₁) · (v₁ × v₂) = 0.
Space curves & vector differentiationFreq: 5/50/5
Arc length, velocity, acceleration
$$\begin{aligned}&s=\int_{t_0}^t|\mathbf{r}'(u)|\,du,\qquad \frac{ds}{dt}=|\mathbf{r}'(t)|\\&\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{r}'=v\mathbf{T},\qquad \mathbf{a}=\mathbf{r}''=a_T\mathbf{T}+a_N\mathbf{N}=\frac{dv}{dt}\mathbf{T}+\kappa v^2\mathbf{N}\end{aligned}$$
Where: a_T = (r' · r'')/|r'| (tangential), a_N = |r' × r''|/|r'| (normal).
Use: Decompose acceleration into tangential and normal parts without computing N explicitly.
Frenet–Serret trihedron (T, N, B)

Moving Trihedron $(\mathbf{T}, \mathbf{N}, \mathbf{B})$ of a Space Curve: Orthonormal right-handed frame formed by the unit tangent $\mathbf{T}$, principal normal $\mathbf{N}$, and binormal $\mathbf{B} = \mathbf{T}\times\mathbf{N}$:

$$\mathbf{T}=\frac{\mathbf{r}'}{|\mathbf{r}'|},\qquad \mathbf{B}=\frac{\mathbf{r}'\times\mathbf{r}''}{|\mathbf{r}'\times\mathbf{r}''|},\qquad \mathbf{N}=\mathbf{B}\times\mathbf{T}=\frac{d\mathbf{T}/dt}{|d\mathbf{T}/dt|}$$
Where: T = unit tangent, N = principal unit normal, B = unit binormal.
Use: In exams, compute T and B first from r' and r' × r'', then get N = B × T (much faster than differentiating T/|T|).
Curvature κ and torsion τ
$$\kappa=\frac{|\mathbf{r}'\times\mathbf{r}''|}{|\mathbf{r}'|^3}=\left|\frac{d\mathbf{T}}{ds}\right|,\qquad \tau=\frac{[\mathbf{r}'\ \mathbf{r}''\ \mathbf{r}''']}{|\mathbf{r}'\times\mathbf{r}''|^2},\qquad \rho=\frac1\kappa,\ \sigma=\frac1\tau$$
Where: ρ = radius of curvature, σ = radius of torsion.
Use: κ = 0 iff the curve is a straight line; τ = 0 iff the curve lies entirely in a plane.
Frenet–Serret formulas & Darboux vector

Frenet–Serret Formulas & Darboux Vector: Rate of change of the orthonormal frame $(\mathbf{T}, \mathbf{N}, \mathbf{B})$ with respect to arc length $s$:

$$\begin{aligned}&\frac{d\mathbf{T}}{ds}=\kappa\mathbf{N},\qquad \frac{d\mathbf{N}}{ds}=-\kappa\mathbf{T}+\tau\mathbf{B},\qquad \frac{d\mathbf{B}}{ds}=-\tau\mathbf{N}\\&\boldsymbol{\omega}=\tau\mathbf{T}+\kappa\mathbf{B}\quad\Big(\frac{d\mathbf{T}}{ds}=\boldsymbol{\omega}\times\mathbf{T},\text{ etc.}\Big)\end{aligned}$$
Where: s = arc-length parameter; ω = Darboux vector.
Use: Standard proof questions: e.g. [T' T'' T'''] = κ³(κτ' − κ'τ) = κ⁵ d/ds(τ/κ).
Osculating, normal & rectifying planes
$$\begin{aligned}&\text{Osculating plane }(\perp\mathbf{B}):\ (\mathbf{R}-\mathbf{r})\cdot(\mathbf{r}'\times\mathbf{r}'')=0\\&\text{Normal plane }(\perp\mathbf{T}):\ (\mathbf{R}-\mathbf{r})\cdot\mathbf{r}'=0\\&\text{Rectifying plane }(\perp\mathbf{N}):\ (\mathbf{R}-\mathbf{r})\cdot\mathbf{N}=0\end{aligned}$$
Where: R = (X, Y, Z) is a general point on the plane; r = r(t₀) is the curve point.
Use: Center of curvature: C = r + ρN. Circular helix r = (a cos t, a sin t, bt): κ = a/(a²+b²), τ = b/(a²+b²).
Gradient, divergence, curl, potentialsFreq: 5/50/6
Gradient & directional derivative
$$\nabla\phi=\hat{\mathbf{i}}\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial x}+\hat{\mathbf{j}}\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial y}+\hat{\mathbf{k}}\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial z},\qquad D_{\hat{\mathbf{u}}}\phi=\nabla\phi\cdot\frac{\mathbf{a}}{|\mathbf{a}|},\qquad \text{max }D_{\hat{\mathbf{u}}}\phi=|\nabla\phi|$$
Where: φ(x,y,z) = scalar field, a = direction vector.
Use: ∇φ points in the direction of maximum rate of increase and is normal to the level surface φ(x,y,z) = c.
Angle between two surfaces & tangent plane
$$\cos\theta=\frac{\nabla\phi_1\cdot\nabla\phi_2}{|\nabla\phi_1||\nabla\phi_2|},\qquad \text{Tangent plane: }(\mathbf{R}-\mathbf{r}_0)\cdot\nabla\phi(\mathbf{r}_0)=0$$
Where: φ₁ = c₁ and φ₂ = c₂ intersecting at r₀.
Use: Surfaces are orthogonal at r₀ iff ∇φ₁ · ∇φ₂ = 0 at r₀.
Divergence & solenoidal fields
$$\nabla\cdot\mathbf{F}=\frac{\partial F_1}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial F_2}{\partial y}+\frac{\partial F_3}{\partial z};\qquad \mathbf{F}\text{ solenoidal}\iff \nabla\cdot\mathbf{F}=0$$
Where: F = (F₁, F₂, F₃).
Use: Measures net outward flux per unit volume. Used constantly in "find constant a so that F is solenoidal".
Curl, irrotational fields & scalar potential
$$\nabla\times\mathbf{F}=\begin{vmatrix}\hat{\mathbf{i}}&\hat{\mathbf{j}}&\hat{\mathbf{k}}\\\partial_x&\partial_y&\partial_z\\F_1&F_2&F_3\end{vmatrix};\qquad \nabla\times\mathbf{F}=\mathbf{0}\iff \mathbf{F}=\nabla\phi\ (\text{conservative})$$
Where: Simply connected domain.
Use: To find φ from F = ∇φ: integrate ∂φ/∂x = F₁, ∂φ/∂y = F₂, ∂φ/∂z = F₃ and match terms without double-counting.
Position-vector identities (r = xi + yj + zk, r = |r|)
$$\begin{aligned}&\nabla r=\frac{\mathbf{r}}{r},\qquad \nabla r^n=nr^{n-2}\mathbf{r},\qquad \nabla f(r)=f'(r)\frac{\mathbf{r}}{r}\\&\nabla\cdot\mathbf{r}=3,\qquad \nabla\times\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{0},\qquad \nabla\cdot(r^n\mathbf{r})=(n+3)r^n,\qquad \nabla^2(r^n)=n(n+1)r^{n-2}\end{aligned}$$
Where: r = √(x² + y² + z²).
Use: Hence r^n r is always irrotational, and is solenoidal iff n = −3; r^n is harmonic (∇²r^n = 0) iff n = 0 or n = −1.
Vector calculus product & second-order identities
$$\begin{aligned}&\nabla\times(\nabla\phi)=\mathbf{0},\qquad \nabla\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf{F})=0,\qquad \nabla\times(\nabla\times\mathbf{F})=\nabla(\nabla\cdot\mathbf{F})-\nabla^2\mathbf{F}\\&\nabla\cdot(\phi\mathbf{F})=\nabla\phi\cdot\mathbf{F}+\phi\nabla\cdot\mathbf{F},\qquad \nabla\times(\phi\mathbf{F})=\nabla\phi\times\mathbf{F}+\phi\nabla\times\mathbf{F}\\&\nabla\cdot(\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B})=\mathbf{B}\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf{A})-\mathbf{A}\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf{B})\end{aligned}$$
Where: φ = scalar field, F, A, B = vector fields with C² components.
Use: Memorise these six identities for proof and simplification problems.
Line, surface & volume integralsFreq: 4/50/3
Line integrals (scalar & work)
$$\int_C\phi\,ds=\int_a^b\phi(\mathbf{r}(t))|\mathbf{r}'(t)|\,dt,\qquad W=\int_C\mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{r}=\int_a^b\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t))\cdot\mathbf{r}'(t)\,dt$$
Where: C parametrised by r(t), a ≤ t ≤ b; dr = dx i + dy j + dz k.
Use: If F = ∇φ is conservative, ∫_C F · dr = φ(B) − φ(A) is path-independent, and ∮_C F · dr = 0 around any closed loop.
Surface area element & flux integral (projection method)
$$\iint_S\mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{S}=\iint_S\mathbf{F}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}}\,dS,\qquad dS=\frac{dx\,dy}{|\hat{\mathbf{n}}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{k}}|}=\frac{dy\,dz}{|\hat{\mathbf{n}}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{i}}|}=\frac{dz\,dx}{|\hat{\mathbf{n}}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{j}}|}$$
Where: n̂ = ±∇g/|∇g| for surface g(x,y,z) = c; for z = f(x,y), n̂ dS = (−f_x i − f_y j + k) dx dy.
Use: Project S onto the coordinate plane where n̂ has a non-zero component; check outward/upward orientation sign.
Parametric surface & volume integrals
$$d\mathbf{S}=(\mathbf{r}_u\times\mathbf{r}_v)\,du\,dv,\qquad \iiint_V\phi\,dV=\iiint_V\phi\,dx\,dy\,dz$$
Where: Cylinder: dx dy dz = r dr dθ dz; Sphere: r² sin φ dr dφ dθ.
Use: Use cylindrical coordinates for cylinders/paraboloids and spherical coordinates for spheres/cones.
Green's, Stokes' and Gauss' theoremsFreq: 5/50/4
Green's theorem in the plane

Green's Theorem in the Plane (Real & Complex Forms): For a positively oriented simple closed curve $C$ bounding region $R$ in the $xy$-plane:

$$\oint_C(P\,dx+Q\,dy)=\iint_R\left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)dx\,dy,\qquad \text{Area}(R)=\frac12\oint_C(x\,dy-y\,dx);\quad \oint_C F(z,\bar{z})\,dz=2i\iint_R\frac{\partial F}{\partial\bar{z}}\,dx\,dy,\qquad \oint_C\bar{z}\,dz=2i\,\text{Area}(R)$$
Where: C = positivamente oriented (counterclockwise) simple closed curve bounding plane region R.
Use: Converts a 2-D closed line integral into a double integral over R (or vice versa for area).
Stokes' (curl) theorem

Stokes' Curl Theorem: Relates the circulation of $\mathbf{F}$ around the closed boundary curve $C=\partial S$ of an oriented open surface $S$ to the surface flux of $\nabla\times\mathbf{F}$:

$$\oint_C\mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{r}=\iint_S(\nabla\times\mathbf{F})\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}}\,dS$$
Where: S = any open smooth surface bounded by closed curve C; orientation of n̂ and C follow the right-hand rule.
Use: Replace a difficult surface integral of ∇×F over a curved cap S by a simpler flat disk S' sharing the same boundary C!
Gauss' divergence theorem

Gauss' Divergence Theorem: Relates the outward flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across a closed surface $S=\partial V$ to the volume integral of $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{F}$ over the enclosed solid $V$:

$$\oiint_S\mathbf{F}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}}\,dS=\iiint_V(\nabla\cdot\mathbf{F})\,dV$$
Where: S = closed surface bounding volume V; n̂ = outward unit normal.
Use: If S is open (e.g. hemisphere without base), close it with a flat cap S_cap, apply Gauss to V, then subtract ∬_{S_cap} F·n̂ dS.
Green's first & second identities (harmonic functions)

Green's First & Second Identities: Derived by applying Gauss's divergence theorem to $\phi\nabla\psi$ and $(\phi\nabla\psi - \psi\nabla\phi)$:

$$\begin{aligned}&\iiint_V(\phi\nabla^2\psi+\nabla\phi\cdot\nabla\psi)dV=\oiint_S\phi\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial n}dS\\&\iiint_V(\phi\nabla^2\psi-\psi\nabla^2\phi)dV=\oiint_S\left(\phi\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial n}-\psi\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial n}\right)dS\end{aligned}$$
Where: ∂ψ/∂n = ∇ψ · n̂ (normal derivative); follows from Gauss applied to φ∇ψ.
Use: Proves uniqueness of Laplace/Poisson equations and that ∯_S (∂φ/∂n) dS = 0 for harmonic φ.
SHM, springs, Lissajous, reduced massFreq: 5/50/6
Simple harmonic motion (SHM) differential equation & kinematics
$$\begin{aligned}&\frac{d^2x}{dt^2}+\omega_0^2x=0,\qquad x=A\sin(\omega_0 t+\phi)\\&v=\omega_0\sqrt{A^2-x^2},\qquad a=-\omega_0^2x,\qquad T=\frac{2\pi}{\omega_0}=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}\end{aligned}$$
Where: A = amplitude, ω₀ = √(k/m) = natural angular frequency, φ = initial phase.
Use: v_max = ω₀A at x = 0; |a_max| = ω₀²A at x = ±A.
Energy & time/space averages in SHM
$$\begin{aligned}&E=K+U=\frac12kA^2=\frac12m\omega_0^2A^2\\&\langle K\rangle_t=\langle U\rangle_t=\frac14kA^2=\frac{E}{2},\qquad \langle K\rangle_x=\frac23E,\quad \langle U\rangle_x=\frac13E\end{aligned}$$
Where: ⟨·⟩_t = time average over one period T; ⟨·⟩_x = position average over [−A, A].
Use: Classic BUET question: prove time-average K equals E/2 while space-average K equals 2E/3.
Compound & torsional pendulums
$$T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{I}{mgd}}=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{k_G^2+d^2}{gd}}=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L_{\text{eq}}}{g}},\qquad T_{\text{torsion}}=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{I}{C}}$$
Where: I = I_G + md² = moment of inertia about pivot, k_G = radius of gyration about CM, L_eq = d + k_G²/d.
Use: Centres of suspension and oscillation are interchangeable (d₁d₂ = k_G², d₁ + d₂ = L_eq); minimum period occurs at d = k_G.
Effective spring constants & massive spring
$$k_{\text{series}}=\left(\sum\frac{1}{k_i}\right)^{-1},\qquad k_{\text{parallel}}=\sum k_i,\qquad T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{M+m_s/3}{k}}$$
Where: m_s = mass of uniform spring, M = attached block mass.
Use: Add 1/3 of the spring mass to the oscillating mass (derived by integrating ½(dm)v(y)² along the spring).
Two-body oscillation & reduced mass
$$\mu=\frac{m_1m_2}{m_1+m_2},\qquad T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{\mu}{k}},\qquad f=\frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{k}{\mu}}$$
Where: μ = reduced mass of m₁ and m₂ connected by spring k on a frictionless surface or diatomic molecule.
Use: Used for diatomic vibrational frequency (HCl, CO) and two blocks connected by a spring.
Superposition of two perpendicular SHMs (Lissajous figures)
$$\frac{x^2}{A^2}+\frac{y^2}{B^2}-\frac{2xy}{AB}\cos\delta=\sin^2\delta$$
Where: x = A sin(ωt), y = B sin(ωt + δ), δ = phase difference.
Use: δ = 0, π ⇒ straight line; δ = ±π/2 ⇒ ellipse aligned with axes (circle if A = B); frequency ratio ω_x : ω_y = tangencies N_y : N_x.
Damped oscillationsFreq: 5/50/3
Damped oscillator equation & general solution
$$m\frac{d^2x}{dt^2}+b\frac{dx}{dt}+kx=0\iff \frac{d^2x}{dt^2}+2\gamma\frac{dx}{dt}+\omega_0^2x=0,\qquad \gamma=\frac{b}{2m},\ \omega_0=\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}$$
Where: b = damping coefficient (F_d = −bv), γ = damping factor (s⁻¹).
Use: Three regimes: underdamped (γ < ω₀), critically damped (γ = ω₀), overdamped (γ > ω₀).
Underdamped oscillation (γ < ω₀)
$$x(t)=A_0e^{-\gamma t}\cos(\omega_d t+\phi),\qquad \omega_d=\sqrt{\omega_0^2-\gamma^2}=\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}-\frac{b^2}{4m^2}},\qquad T_d=\frac{2\pi}{\omega_d}$$
Where: A(t) = A₀ e^{−γt} = decaying amplitude envelope, ω_d = damped angular frequency.
Use: For light damping (γ ≪ ω₀), ω_d ≈ ω₀(1 − γ²/2ω₀²).
Energy decay, relaxation time, logarithmic decrement & Q-factor
$$\begin{aligned}&E(t)=E_0e^{-2\gamma t}=E_0e^{-t/\tau},\qquad \tau=\frac{1}{2\gamma}=\frac{m}{b}\\&\lambda=\ln\frac{A(t)}{A(t+T_d)}=\gamma T_d=\frac1N\ln\frac{A_0}{A_N},\qquad Q=2\pi\frac{E}{|\Delta E|_T}=\frac{\omega_0}{2\gamma}=\omega_0\tau=\frac{\pi}{\lambda}\end{aligned}$$
Where: τ = energy relaxation (modulus of decay) time; λ = logarithmic decrement; Q = quality factor.
Use: Note amplitude decays as e^{−γt} while energy decays twice as fast as e^{−2γt}!
Forced oscillations & resonanceFreq: 5/50/3
Driven oscillator steady-state amplitude & phase
$$\begin{aligned}&\frac{d^2x}{dt^2}+2\gamma\frac{dx}{dt}+\omega_0^2x=\frac{F_0}{m}\sin(\omega t)\implies x(t)=A(\omega)\sin(\omega t-\delta)\\&A(\omega)=\frac{F_0/m}{\sqrt{(\omega_0^2-\omega^2)^2+4\gamma^2\omega^2}},\qquad \tan\delta=\frac{2\gamma\omega}{\omega_0^2-\omega^2}\end{aligned}$$
Where: ω = driving angular frequency, δ = phase lag of displacement behind driving force.
Use: At ω ≪ ω₀, A ≈ F₀/k (stiffness controlled, δ ≈ 0); at ω = ω₀, δ = π/2; at ω ≫ ω₀, δ → π.
Amplitude resonance vs velocity/power resonance
$$\begin{aligned}&\text{Amplitude resonance: }\omega_r=\sqrt{\omega_0^2-2\gamma^2},\qquad A_{\max}=\frac{F_0/m}{2\gamma\sqrt{\omega_0^2-\gamma^2}}\\&\text{Velocity / Power resonance: }\omega=\omega_0,\qquad v_{\max}=\frac{F_0}{b},\qquad \langle P\rangle_{\max}=\frac{F_0^2}{2b}\end{aligned}$$
Where: Amplitude peaks slightly below ω₀; velocity and average absorbed power peak exactly at ω = ω₀.
Use: Distinguish carefully between ω₀ (velocity resonance), √(ω₀² − γ²) (free damped), and √(ω₀² − 2γ²) (amplitude resonance).
Average power absorbed, bandwidth & sharpness of resonance
$$\langle P(\omega)\rangle=\frac{F_0^2\gamma\omega^2/m}{(\omega_0^2-\omega^2)^2+4\gamma^2\omega^2},\qquad \Delta\omega_{\text{FWHM}}=2\gamma=\frac{b}{m},\qquad Q=\frac{\omega_0}{\Delta\omega}=\frac{\omega_0}{2\gamma}$$
Where: Δω = full width at half-maximum power (half-power points where ⟨P⟩ = ½⟨P⟩_max).
Use: Higher Q means narrower bandwidth Δω and sharper resonance peak.
Waves: velocity, group velocity, standing waves, beats, DopplerFreq: 4/50/5
Progressive wave equation & wave speeds
$$\begin{aligned}&y(x,t)=A\sin(kx-\omega t+\phi),\qquad \frac{\partial^2y}{\partial x^2}=\frac{1}{v^2}\frac{\partial^2y}{\partial t^2},\qquad k=\frac{2\pi}{\lambda},\ v=\frac{\omega}{k}=f\lambda\\&v_{\text{string}}=\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}},\qquad v_{\text{bar}}=\sqrt{\frac{Y}{\rho}},\qquad v_{\text{sound}}=\sqrt{\frac{B}{\rho}}=\sqrt{\frac{\gamma P}{\rho}}=\sqrt{\frac{\gamma RT}{M}}\end{aligned}$$
Where: k = 2π/λ = wavenumber, μ = linear mass density, γ = C_p/C_v (Laplace adiabatic correction).
Use: Particle velocity v_p = ∂y/∂t = −v(∂y/∂x); maximum particle velocity = ωA.
Energy density, power & intensity of a wave
$$u=\frac{dE}{dV}=\frac12\rho\omega^2A^2=2\pi^2\rho f^2A^2,\qquad P=\frac12\mu\omega^2A^2v,\qquad I=\frac{P}{S}=\frac12\rho v\omega^2A^2=\frac{p_0^2}{2\rho v}$$
Where: ρ = medium density, v = wave speed, p₀ = B k A = ρ v ω A = pressure amplitude.
Use: Intensity I ∝ f² A²; spherical wave amplitude falls off as A ∝ 1/r so I ∝ 1/r².
Phase velocity vs group velocity (dispersion relation)
$$v_p=\frac{\omega}{k},\qquad v_g=\frac{d\omega}{dk}=v_p+k\frac{dv_p}{dk}=v_p-\lambda\frac{dv_p}{d\lambda}$$
Where: v_p = speed of individual ripples, v_g = speed of wave packet envelope / energy transport.
Use: Normal dispersion: dv_p/dλ > 0 ⇒ v_g < v_p. Relativistic de Broglie wave: v_p v_g = c².
Standing waves & normal modes (strings and organ pipes)
$$y=2A\sin(kx)\cos(\omega t),\qquad f_n=\frac{nv}{2L}\ (n=1,2,3,\dots\text{ fixed ends / open pipe}),\qquad f_n=\frac{(2n-1)v}{4L}\ (\text{closed pipe})$$
Where: Distance between adjacent nodes (or antinodes) = λ/2; node to adjacent antinode = λ/4.
Use: With end correction e = 0.6r: L_eff = L + 2e (open pipe) or L + e (closed at one end).
Beats & acoustic Doppler effect
$$f_{\text{beat}}=|f_1-f_2|,\qquad f'=f\left(\frac{v+v_w\pm v_O}{v+v_w\mp v_S}\right)$$
Where: v = sound speed, v_w = wind speed along S→O; top signs = observer/source moving toward each other.
Use: Remember top signs ("toward") increase frequency; bottom signs ("away") decrease frequency.
Interference (Young, biprism, Lloyd, thin films, Newton's rings, Michelson)Freq: 5/50/5
Resultant intensity & visibility of two coherent waves
$$\begin{aligned}&I=I_1+I_2+2\sqrt{I_1I_2}\cos\delta,\qquad I=4I_0\cos^2\!\left(\frac{\delta}{2}\right)\ (I_1=I_2=I_0)\\&\delta=\frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\Delta,\qquad \frac{I_{\max}}{I_{\min}}=\left(\frac{a_1+a_2}{a_1-a_2}\right)^2,\qquad V=\frac{I_{\max}-I_{\min}}{I_{\max}+I_{\min}}=\frac{2\sqrt{I_1I_2}}{I_1+I_2}\end{aligned}$$
Where: δ = phase difference, Δ = optical path difference = n · (geometric path).
Use: Constructive: Δ = mλ (δ = 2mπ); Destructive: Δ = (m + ½)λ (δ = (2m+1)π).
Young's double-slit, Fresnel biprism & mica sheet shift
$$\begin{aligned}&y_m=\frac{m\lambda D}{d},\qquad \beta=\frac{\lambda D}{d},\qquad \Delta y=\frac{D}{d}(\mu-1)t=\frac{\beta}{\lambda}(\mu-1)t\\&\text{Fresnel biprism: }d=2a(\mu-1)\alpha=\sqrt{d_1d_2}\quad(\text{displacement method})\end{aligned}$$
Where: d = slit separation, D = slit-to-screen distance, β = fringe width, t = thickness of film of index μ.
Use: Inserting a plate of thickness t and index μ shifts the central fringe by N = (μ − 1)t/λ fringes toward that slit.
Thin-film interference (parallel & wedge-shaped films)
$$2\mu t\cos r=\begin{cases}(m+\frac12)\lambda & \text{reflected bright / transmitted dark}\\m\lambda & \text{reflected dark / transmitted bright}\end{cases},\qquad \beta_{\text{wedge}}=\frac{\lambda}{2\mu\theta\cos r}\approx\frac{\lambda}{2\mu\theta}$$
Where: t = film thickness, r = angle of refraction inside film, θ = wedge angle (in radians).
Use: Assumes one reflection undergoes a π (λ/2) phase change (air–glass–air). If n₁ < n_film < n_substrate (anti-reflection coating), both reflections shift by π so destructive reflection is 2μt = (m + ½)λ ⇒ t_min = λ/(4μ).
Newton's rings (reflected light)
$$\begin{aligned}&D_m^2=4m\lambda R\ (\text{dark}),\qquad D_m^2=2(2m-1)\lambda R\ (\text{bright})\\&\lambda=\frac{D_{m+p}^2-D_m^2}{4pR},\qquad \mu_{\text{liq}}=\frac{(D_{m+p}^2-D_m^2)_{\text{air}}}{(D_{m+p}^2-D_m^2)_{\text{liq}}}\end{aligned}$$
Where: D_m = diameter of m-th ring, R = radius of curvature of lens, p = ring-count interval.
Use: Taking differences D_{m+p}² − D_m² eliminates unknown zero-order contact error at the center!
Michelson interferometer
$$2d\cos\theta=m\lambda,\qquad \Delta d=\frac{N\lambda}{2},\qquad (\mu-1)t=\frac{N\lambda}{2},\qquad \Delta\lambda=\frac{\lambda^2}{2\,\Delta d}$$
Where: Δd = mirror translation shifting N fringes; Δλ = wavelength doublet spacing (e.g. Na D₁, D₂) giving Δd between contrast minima.
Use: Each fringe shift corresponds to λ/2 of mirror travel.
Diffraction: slit, double slit, grating, circular aperture, resolving powerFreq: 5/50/4
Fraunhofer single-slit diffraction
$$\begin{aligned}&I(\theta)=I_0\left(\frac{\sin\alpha}{\alpha}\right)^2,\qquad \alpha=\frac{\pi a\sin\theta}{\lambda}\\&\text{Minima: }a\sin\theta=m\lambda\ (m=\pm1,\pm2,\dots),\qquad w_{\text{central}}=\frac{2\lambda f}{a}\end{aligned}$$
Where: a = slit width, f = focal length of lens (or screen distance D).
Use: Secondary maxima occur at tan α = α ⇒ α ≈ ±1.430π, ±2.459π (intensities ≈ I₀/22.2, I₀/61.7).
Double-slit diffraction & missing orders
$$I(\theta)=4I_0\left(\frac{\sin\alpha}{\alpha}\right)^2\cos^2\beta,\qquad \alpha=\frac{\pi a\sin\theta}{\lambda},\quad \beta=\frac{\pi(a+b)\sin\theta}{\lambda},\qquad \frac{a+b}{a}=\frac{n}{m}\ (\text{missing order})$$
Where: a = slit width, b = opaque separation, d = a + b = slit-center spacing.
Use: The n-th interference maximum (d sin θ = nλ) is missing when it coincides with the m-th diffraction minimum (a sin θ = mλ).
Diffraction grating (N slits): principal maxima, dispersion & resolving power
$$\begin{aligned}&(a+b)\sin\theta=n\lambda,\qquad n_{\max}=\left\lfloor\frac{a+b}{\lambda}\right\rfloor\\&\text{Dispersive power: }\frac{d\theta}{d\lambda}=\frac{n}{(a+b)\cos\theta},\qquad \text{Resolving power: }R=\frac{\lambda}{\Delta\lambda}=nN\end{aligned}$$
Where: a + b = 1/N_lines = grating element (e.g. 1 cm / 6000 lines), N = total illuminated rulings, n = spectral order.
Use: Half-width of principal maximum: Δθ = λ/(N(a+b)cos θ). Between two principal maxima there are N − 1 minima and N − 2 secondary maxima.
Circular aperture, Rayleigh criterion & Bragg X-ray diffraction
$$\theta_{\min}=\frac{1.22\lambda}{D},\qquad R_{\text{telescope}}=\frac{D}{1.22\lambda},\qquad R_{\text{prism}}=b\frac{d\mu}{d\lambda},\qquad 2d\sin\theta=n\lambda\ (\text{Bragg})$$
Where: D = lens/aperture diameter, θ = glancing angle for Bragg crystal planes of spacing d.
Use: Note θ in Bragg's law is the glancing angle (with the crystal plane), whereas in grating diffraction θ is measured from the normal!
Polarisation, double refraction, optical activityFreq: 5/50/3
Brewster's law & Malus's law
$$\tan\theta_p=\frac{n_2}{n_1}=\mu,\qquad \theta_p+r=90^\circ,\qquad I=I_0\cos^2\theta$$
Where: θ_p = polarising (Brewster) angle, r = angle of refraction, θ = angle between transmission axes of polariser and analyser.
Use: Unpolarised light of intensity I_unpol passing through an ideal polariser emerges with intensity ½ I_unpol.
Double refraction (birefringence) & wave plates
$$\Delta=t|n_o-n_e|,\qquad t_{\text{QWP}}=\frac{\lambda}{4|n_o-n_e|}\text{ or }\frac{(2m+1)\lambda}{4|n_o-n_e|},\qquad t_{\text{HWP}}=\frac{(2m+1)\lambda}{2|n_o-n_e|}$$
Where: n_o, n_e = refractive indices of O-ray and E-ray (calcite: n_o > n_e, negative crystal; quartz: n_e > n_o, positive crystal).
Use: Quarter-wave plate (QWP) at 45° to linear polarisation converts linear ↔ circular light; half-wave plate (HWP) rotates plane of polarisation by 2θ.
Optical activity & specific rotation (polarimeter)
$$\theta=S\,l\,c,\qquad S=\frac{\theta}{l\cdot c}\quad\text{(in deg}\cdot\text{dm}^{-1}\cdot\text{g}^{-1}\cdot\text{cm}^3\text{)}$$
Where: θ = optical rotation (degrees), l = tube length in decimetres (1 dm = 10 cm!), c = concentration in g/cm³.
Use: Watch the unit of length l: specific rotation S is almost always given per decimetre (dm), so divide l(cm) by 10!
Lens aberrations, dispersion, achromatismFreq: 3/50/2
Dispersive power & chromatic aberration of a thin lens
$$\omega=\frac{\mu_V-\mu_R}{\mu_Y-1},\qquad \frac{f_R-f_V}{f_Y}=\omega\implies \Delta f=f_R-f_V=\omega f_Y$$
Where: μ_V, μ_R, μ_Y = refractive indices for violet, red, and mean yellow light (μ_Y = ½(μ_V + μ_R)).
Use: Longitudinal chromatic aberration for parallel rays equals ωf.
Achromatic doublet (in contact and separated by distance d)
$$\text{Contact: }\frac{\omega_1}{f_1}+\frac{\omega_2}{f_2}=0,\quad \frac{1}{F}=\frac{1}{f_1}+\frac{1}{f_2};\qquad \text{Separated (same glass): }d=\frac{f_1+f_2}{2}$$
Where: f₁, f₂ = focal lengths of the two lenses, ω₁, ω₂ = dispersive powers.
Use: For contact doublet, one lens must be converging and the other diverging (opposite signs of f₁, f₂). For Huygens eyepiece (f₁ = 3f, f₂ = f), d = 2f satisfies both achromatism and minimum spherical aberration (f₁ − f₂ = d).
Thermodynamic processes, Carnot cycle, second lawFreq: 5/50/3
First law of thermodynamics & molar heat capacities
$$dQ=dU+dW=dU+P\,dV,\qquad dU=nC_v\,dT,\qquad C_p-C_v=R,\qquad \gamma=\frac{C_p}{C_v}=1+\frac{2}{f},\qquad C_v=\frac{f}{2}R$$
Where: f = degrees of freedom (3 monatomic, 5 diatomic, 6 polyatomic); U depends only on T for an ideal gas.
Use: dU = nC_v dT holds for ANY process of an ideal gas (even constant pressure or adiabatic)!
Work done in isothermal, adiabatic, isobaric & polytropic processes
$$\begin{aligned}&W_{\text{iso}}=nRT\ln\frac{V_2}{V_1}=nRT\ln\frac{P_1}{P_2},\qquad \Delta U_{\text{iso}}=0\\&PV^\gamma=\text{const},\quad TV^{\gamma-1}=\text{const},\quad P^{1-\gamma}T^\gamma=\text{const}\\&W_{\text{adiab}}=\frac{P_1V_1-P_2V_2}{\gamma-1}=\frac{nR(T_1-T_2)}{\gamma-1}=-\Delta U\end{aligned}$$
Where: Slope of adiabatic on P–V diagram is γ times steeper than isothermal: (dP/dV)_adiab = −γ(P/V).
Use: Convert log₁₀ to ln via ln x = 2.3026 log₁₀ x if you prefer, or evaluate ln directly.
Carnot heat engine, refrigerator & heat pump
$$\eta=1-\frac{Q_C}{Q_H}=1-\frac{T_C}{T_H}=\frac{W}{Q_H},\qquad \text{COP}_{\text{ref}}=\frac{Q_C}{W}=\frac{T_C}{T_H-T_C},\qquad \text{COP}_{\text{HP}}=\frac{Q_H}{W}=\frac{T_H}{T_H-T_C}=\text{COP}_{\text{ref}}+1$$
Where: T_H, T_C MUST be in Kelvin (K = °C + 273.15)!
Use: Lowering T_C by ΔT increases Carnot efficiency more than raising T_H by the same ΔT because ∂η/∂T_C = −1/T_H whereas ∂η/∂T_H = T_C/T_H².
EntropyFreq: 5/50/3
Clausius theorem, entropy definition & T–S diagram
$$\oint\frac{\delta Q}{T}\le0,\qquad dS=\frac{\delta Q_{\text{rev}}}{T},\qquad \Delta S_{\text{univ}}=\Delta S_{\text{sys}}+\Delta S_{\text{surr}}\ge0,\qquad Q_{\text{rev}}=\int T\,dS$$
Where: Equality (= 0) holds for reversible cycles; strict inequality for irreversible cycles.
Use: Because S is a state function, compute ΔS of an irreversible process by devising any convenient reversible path between the same initial and final states!
Entropy change of an ideal gas (3 equivalent forms)
$$\begin{aligned}\Delta S&=nC_v\ln\frac{T_2}{T_1}+nR\ln\frac{V_2}{V_1}\\&=nC_p\ln\frac{T_2}{T_1}-nR\ln\frac{P_2}{P_1}\\&=nC_v\ln\frac{P_2}{P_1}+nC_p\ln\frac{V_2}{V_1}\end{aligned}$$
Where: Free expansion into vacuum (T₂ = T₁): ΔS_gas = nR ln(V₂/V₁), ΔS_surr = 0.
Use: Pick the form matching the two given state variables: (T,V), (T,P), or (P,V).
Entropy change in heating, phase change & mixing
$$\Delta S_{\text{heating}}=mc\ln\frac{T_2}{T_1},\qquad \Delta S_{\text{phase}}=\frac{mL}{T_{\text{tr}}},\qquad \Delta S_{\text{mix}}=-R\sum n_i\ln x_i$$
Where: c = specific heat, L = latent heat of fusion/vaporisation at transition temperature T_tr (in K), x_i = mole fraction.
Use: For ice at T₁ < 273 K turning into steam at T₂ > 373 K, sum mc_ice ln(273/T₁) + mL_f/273 + mc_w ln(373/273) + mL_v/373 + mc_s ln(T₂/373).
Thermodynamic potentials, Maxwell relations, Clausius–ClapeyronFreq: 5/50/4
Four thermodynamic potentials & differential forms
$$\begin{aligned}&dU=T\,dS-P\,dV\\&dH=T\,dS+V\,dP\quad(H=U+PV)\\&dF=-S\,dT-P\,dV\quad(F=U-TS,\text{ Helmholtz})\\&dG=-S\,dT+V\,dP\quad(G=H-TS,\text{ Gibbs})\end{aligned}$$
Where: Natural variables: U(S,V), H(S,P), F(T,V), G(T,P).
Use: At constant (T, P), spontaneous processes decrease Gibbs free energy G (equilibrium ⇔ dG = 0).
The four Maxwell thermodynamic relations
$$\begin{aligned}&\left(\frac{\partial T}{\partial V}\right)_S=-\left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial S}\right)_V,\qquad \left(\frac{\partial T}{\partial P}\right)_S=\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial S}\right)_P\\&\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial V}\right)_T=\left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial T}\right)_V,\qquad \left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial P}\right)_T=-\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_P\end{aligned}$$
Where: Derived from equality of mixed second partials ∂²Φ/∂x∂y = ∂²Φ/∂y∂x.
Use: Mnemonic: "Good Physicists Have Studied Under Very Fine Teachers" or cross-multiply (T,S) vs (P,V) with minus sign when S and V are on the same side.
TdS equations, internal energy equation & C_p − C_v general relation
$$\begin{aligned}&T\,dS=C_v\,dT+T\left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial T}\right)_V dV=C_p\,dT-T\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_P dP\\&\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial V}\right)_T=T\left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial T}\right)_V-P,\qquad C_p-C_v=T\left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial T}\right)_V\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_P=\frac{TV\alpha^2}{\kappa_T}\end{aligned}$$
Where: α = (1/V)(∂V/∂T)_P = volume expansivity, κ_T = −(1/V)(∂V/∂P)_T = isothermal compressibility.
Use: For a van der Waals gas (P + a/V²)(V − b) = RT, (∂U/∂V)_T = a/V² and C_p − C_v ≈ R(1 + 2a/RTV).
Clausius–Clapeyron latent heat equation & Joule–Thomson coefficient
$$\frac{dP}{dT}=\frac{L}{T(v_2-v_1)},\qquad \mu_{JT}=\left(\frac{\partial T}{\partial P}\right)_H=\frac{1}{C_p}\left[T\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_P-V\right],\qquad T_i=\frac{2a}{Rb}$$
Where: L = specific latent heat, v₁, v₂ = specific volumes of phases 1 and 2; T_i = inversion temperature of van der Waals gas.
Use: For water→ice, v_ice > v_water so dP/dT < 0 (melting point drops under pressure). For steam, v₂ ≫ v₁ gives ln(P₂/P₁) = (M L/R)(1/T₁ − 1/T₂).
Kinetic theory, equipartition, mean free path, real gasesFreq: 4/50/3
Kinetic pressure & Maxwell–Boltzmann molecular speeds
$$\begin{aligned}&P=\frac13\rho v_{\text{rms}}^2=\frac23\frac{E_{\text{tr}}}{V}\\&v_{\text{mp}}=\sqrt{\frac{2RT}{M}},\qquad \bar{v}=\sqrt{\frac{8RT}{\pi M}},\qquad v_{\text{rms}}=\sqrt{\frac{3RT}{M}}\quad(v_{\text{mp}}:\bar{v}:v_{\text{rms}}=1:1.128:1.225)\end{aligned}$$
Where: M = molar mass MUST be in kg/mol (e.g. O₂ = 0.032 kg/mol, N₂ = 0.028 kg/mol)!
Use: Translational kinetic energy of 1 molecule = (3/2)k_B T, regardless of molar mass.
Mean free path, collision frequency & transport coefficients
$$\lambda=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}\pi n d^2}=\frac{k_BT}{\sqrt{2}\pi d^2 P},\qquad Z=\frac{\bar{v}}{\lambda}=\sqrt{2}\pi n d^2\bar{v},\qquad \eta=\frac13\rho\bar{v}\lambda,\qquad K=\frac13\rho\bar{v}\lambda c_v=\eta c_v$$
Where: n = P/(k_B T) = number density (molecules/m³), d = molecular diameter, η = viscosity, K = thermal conductivity.
Use: At constant T, λ ∝ 1/P; dynamic viscosity η = (1/3)m v̄ / (√2 π d²) is independent of pressure P and scales as √T!
Van der Waals equation & critical constants
$$\left(P+\frac{n^2a}{V^2}\right)(V-nb)=nRT,\qquad V_c=3b,\qquad P_c=\frac{a}{27b^2},\qquad T_c=\frac{8a}{27Rb},\qquad Z_c=\frac{P_cV_c}{RT_c}=\frac38=0.375$$
Where: a accounts for intermolecular attraction; b = 4 N_A (4/3 π r³) = 4 × molecular volume.
Use: Boyle temperature (where gas behaves ideally at low P): T_B = a/(Rb) = (27/8)T_c; inversion temperature T_i = 2T_B = 2a/(Rb).
Acoustics, reverberation, intensity levelFreq: 3/50/1
Sound intensity level (dB) & Sabine reverberation formula
$$\beta=10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{I}{I_0}\right)\text{ dB}\quad(I_0=10^{-12}\text{ W/m}^2),\qquad T_{60}=\frac{0.161\,V}{A}=\frac{0.161\,V}{\sum \alpha_i S_i}$$
Where: V = hall volume in m³, α_i = absorption coefficient of surface S_i (m²), A = ∑ α_i S_i = total absorption in metric sabins (OWU).
Use: T_60 is the time for sound intensity to drop by 60 dB (to 10⁻⁶ of initial value). Eyring formula for dead rooms: T_60 = 0.161 V / [−S ln(1 − ᾱ)].
C basics: types, operators, printf, control flowFreq: 5/50/3
Standard C data types & format specifiers
TypeBytes (64-bit)FormatRange / Notes
char / unsigned char1%c / %hhu−128..127 / 0..255
int / unsigned int4%d / %u−2.14×10⁹ .. 2.14×10⁹
long long8%lld≈ ±9.22×10¹⁸
float / double4 / 8%f / %lf~7 digits / ~15 digits precision
Where: In printf, %f prints both float and double; in scanf, double requires %lf while float requires %f.
Use: Use %05d for zero-padded width 5; %-8.2f for left-aligned width 8 with 2 decimals.
Operator precedence, short-circuit evaluation & sequence points
// Short-circuit: RHS of && not evaluated if LHS is 0; RHS of || not evaluated if LHS is non-zero
int a = 0, b = 5;
if (a != 0 && (b / a) > 1) { /* safe: b/a skipped */ }
// Post-increment vs Pre-increment:
int x = 5, y = x++; // y = 5, x = 6
int z = ++x;        // x = 7, z = 7
Where: Precedence high → low: () [] -> . > ++ -- ! ~ * & (unary) > * / % > + - > << >> > < <= > >= > == != > & > ^ > | > && > || > ?: > = +=.
Use: Integer division truncates toward zero (7 / 2 == 3, -7 / 2 == -3); sign of a % b matches the dividend a (-7 % 3 == -1).
Switch-case fallthrough, break & continue
switch (grade) {
    case 'A': case 'a': pts = 4; break;
    case 'B': case 'b': pts = 3; break;
    default:            pts = 0; break;
}
Where: Switch expression must be an integer/char/enum type (never float or string).
Use: Omitting break causes execution to fall through into the next case label.
Standard-library quick referenceFreq: 3/50/1
Common C headers: <stdio.h>, <stdlib.h>, <string.h>, <ctype.h>, <math.h>
HeaderKey Functions
<string.h>strlen(s), strcpy(d,s), strncpy(d,s,n), strcat(d,s), strcmp(a,b), strchr(s,c), strstr(h,n), memcpy(d,s,n)
<ctype.h>isalpha(c), isdigit(c), isalnum(c), isspace(c), isupper(c), tolower(c), toupper(c)
<stdlib.h>malloc(sz), calloc(n,sz), realloc(p,sz), free(p), atoi(s), atof(s), qsort(...), abs(x)

Where: strcmp(a, b) returns < 0 if a < b lexicographically, 0 if equal, > 0 if a > b.
Use: Never compare C strings with a == b (that compares pointer addresses); always use strcmp(a, b) == 0.
Pointers, dynamic memory, call by value / address, 2D allocationFreq: 5/50/3
Pointer arithmetic, array decay & const pointers
int a[5] = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50};
int *p = a;              // p points to a[0]; *(p + i) == a[i]
const int *p1 = a;       // data is const (*p1 = 99 illegal), pointer can move (p1++ legal)
int *const p2 = a;       // pointer is const (p2++ illegal), data can change (*p2 = 99 legal)
Where: Adding 1 to int *p advances the byte address by sizeof(int) (typically 4 bytes).
Use: *p++ increments the pointer p and yields the old *p; (*p)++ increments the value pointed to by p.
Call by address (swap) & function pointers
void swap(int *x, int *y) {
    int t = *x; *x = *y; *y = t;
}
int apply(int (*op)(int, int), int a, int b) {
    return op(a, b);
}
Where: Pass &a, &b to swap(&a, &b).
Use: Write parentheses carefully: int (*fp)(int, int) is a pointer to a function; int *fp(int, int) is a function returning int*.
Dynamic 2-D array allocation & deallocation (malloc / free)
int **mat = (int **)malloc(R * sizeof(int *));
for (int i = 0; i < R; i++)
    mat[i] = (int *)malloc(C * sizeof(int));
// ... use mat[i][j] ...
for (int i = 0; i < R; i++)
    free(mat[i]);
free(mat);
Where: R = rows, C = columns. Always free rows in reverse order before freeing the row-pointer array!
Use: Very frequent BUET CSE 109 question: allocate a jagged or R×C matrix dynamically, read/multiply, and free without memory leaks.
Linked lists & binary search trees (basics)Freq: 4/50/2
Singly linked list node, insert, delete & reverse
typedef struct Node {
    int data;
    struct Node *next;
} Node;

Node* reverseList(Node *head) {
    Node *prev = NULL, *curr = head, *nxt = NULL;
    while (curr != NULL) {
        nxt = curr->next;
        curr->next = prev;
        prev = curr;
        curr = nxt;
    }
    return prev;
}
Where: Self-referential struct must use the struct tag (struct Node *next) inside its own body.
Use: Always handle the empty list (head == NULL) and head deletion as special cases.
Binary search tree (BST) node, insert & inorder traversal
typedef struct TNode {
    int key;
    struct TNode *left, *right;
} TNode;

TNode* insert(TNode *root, int k) {
    if (!root) {
        TNode *n = (TNode*)malloc(sizeof(TNode));
        n->key = k; n->left = n->right = NULL;
        return n;
    }
    if (k < root->key) root->left  = insert(root->left, k);
    else               root->right = insert(root->right, k);
    return root;
}
Where: BST property: all keys in left subtree < root->key < all keys in right subtree.
Use: Inorder traversal (left, root, right) of a BST visits keys in sorted ascending order.
Arrays & strings (manual implementations)Freq: 5/50/2
Manual strlen, strcpy, strcat, strcmp & in-place reverse (no <string.h>)
int my_strlen(const char *s) {
    const char *p = s;
    while (*p) p++;
    return p - s;
}
int my_strcmp(const char *a, const char *b) {
    while (*a && (*a == *b)) { a++; b++; }
    return (unsigned char)*a - (unsigned char)*b;
}
void rev_str(char *s) {
    int i = 0, j = my_strlen(s) - 1;
    while (i < j) { char t = s[i]; s[i++] = s[j]; s[j--] = t; }
}
Where: C strings are null-terminated ('\0' == 0); array size must be at least length + 1.
Use: Exam questions routinely state "Write a function without using any library string functions".
Substring search & word/token extraction
int find_sub(const char *str, const char *sub) {
    for (int i = 0; str[i]; i++) {
        int j = 0;
        while (sub[j] && str[i + j] == sub[j]) j++;
        if (!sub[j]) return i; // first match index
    }
    return -1;
}
Where: Returns starting 0-based index of sub inside str, or −1 if not found.
Use: To delete all occurrences of a word or compress spaces, maintain separate read (i) and write (k) indices in one pass.
Structures & file I/OFreq: 5/50/2
Structs, arrays of structs & arrow operator (->)
typedef struct {
    int id;
    char name[40];
    double cgpa;
} Student;

void update(Student *s, double g) {
    s->cgpa = g; // equivalent to (*s).cgpa = g;
}
Where: Use dot (s.cgpa) on a struct variable and arrow (p->cgpa) on a struct pointer.
Use: Structs are passed by value in C unless you pass a pointer (Student *s).
Text & binary file I/O (fopen, fscanf, fprintf, fread, fwrite, fseek)
FILE *fp = fopen("input.txt", "r");
if (fp == NULL) return 1;
int x;
while (fscanf(fp, "%d", &x) == 1) {
    /* process x */
}
// Binary read/write of N structs:
fwrite(arr, sizeof(Student), N, binFp);
fseek(binFp, k * sizeof(Student), SEEK_SET); // jump to k-th record
fclose(fp);
Where: Modes: "r", "w", "a", "r+", "rb", "wb". fseek origins: SEEK_SET (start), SEEK_CUR (current), SEEK_END (end).
Use: Check fscanf(...) == expected_count rather than while(!feof(fp)) to avoid processing the last line twice!
Bitwise operators, unions, enumsFreq: 5/50/2
Bitwise masks: test, set, clear, toggle & extract bitfields
unsigned int x;
int bit = (x >> k) & 1U;       // test k-th bit (0-indexed from LSB)
x |=  (1U << k);               // set k-th bit to 1
x &= ~(1U << k);               // clear k-th bit to 0
x ^=  (1U << k);               // toggle k-th bit
int isPow2 = (x > 0) && ((x & (x - 1)) == 0); // power of 2 check
int popcnt = 0; while (x) { x &= (x - 1); popcnt++; } // Kernighan set-bit count
Where: Use unsigned types when shifting right (>> on unsigned is logical zero-fill shift).
Use: Circular left rotate of 32-bit unsigned x by n bits: (x << n) | (x >> (32 - n)).
Unions, bit-fields & enumerations
union Data { int i; float f; unsigned char bytes[4]; }; // sizeof == max member (4)
struct Flags { unsigned int ready : 1; unsigned int mode : 3; };
enum Color { RED = 1, GREEN, BLUE }; // GREEN == 2, BLUE == 3
Where: All members of a union share the same memory address; modifying one overwrites the others.
Use: A union with unsigned char bytes[4] and int i is used to inspect byte order (little-endian vs big-endian).
Number systems, ASCII & type conversionFreq: 3/50/1
ASCII ranges, character conversion & two's complement
$$\text{'0'}=48,\quad \text{'A'}=65,\quad \text{'a'}=97,\quad \text{digit}=c-\text{'0'},\quad \text{lower}=c-\text{'A'}+\text{'a'}\ (=c\mid 32)$$
Where: In two's complement, −x = (~x) + 1; range of n-bit signed integer is −2^{n−1} to 2^{n−1} − 1.
Use: Convert char digit to int via c - '0'; convert uppercase to lowercase via c + ('a' - 'A').
Functions, recursion & standard programsFreq: 5/50/2
Recursion: GCD (Euclid), binary search, Fibonacci & Tower of Hanoi
int gcd(int a, int b) { return b == 0 ? a : gcd(b, a % b); }

int binSearch(int a[], int lo, int hi, int key) {
    if (lo > hi) return -1;
    int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
    if (a[mid] == key) return mid;
    return (key < a[mid]) ? binSearch(a, lo, mid - 1, key)
                          : binSearch(a, mid + 1, hi, key);
}
Where: Every recursive function needs a base case that stops recursion and a step that shrinks the state.
Use: LCM(a, b) = (a / gcd(a, b)) * b (divide first to avoid integer overflow).
Sorting (Bubble / Selection) & prime sieve / check
void bubbleSort(int a[], int n) {
    for (int i = 0; i < n - 1; i++)
        for (int j = 0; j < n - 1 - i; j++)
            if (a[j] > a[j + 1]) { int t = a[j]; a[j] = a[j+1]; a[j+1] = t; }
}
int isPrime(int n) {
    if (n < 2) return 0;
    for (int d = 2; d * d <= n; d++) if (n % d == 0) return 0;
    return 1;
}
Where: Prime check only needs to test divisors up to d * d <= n.
Use: Used inside array filtering, custom comparator sorting, and Goldbach/twin-prime problems.
Common programming patterns (digits, patterns, matrices, series)Freq: 4/50/1
Digit extraction, palindrome number, base conversion & matrix multiplication
// Reverse integer / extract digits in base b (use b = 10 for decimal, b = 2 for binary):
int rev = 0, temp = n;
while (temp > 0) { rev = rev * 10 + (temp % 10); temp /= 10; }

// Matrix multiplication C[m][p] = A[m][n] * B[n][p]:
for (int i = 0; i < m; i++)
    for (int j = 0; j < p; j++) {
        C[i][j] = 0;
        for (int k = 0; k < n; k++) C[i][j] += A[i][k] * B[k][j];
    }
Where: For Taylor series (e.g. cos x = 1 − x²/2! + x⁴/4! − …), compute each term from the previous term: term *= -x*x / ((2*k-1)*(2*k)) instead of calling pow() and fact()!
Use: Recurrence update for series terms avoids factorial overflow and gets full marks.
C++: classes, copy control, operator overloading, inheritance, polymorphismFreq: 5/50/3
Rule of Three: constructor, deep copy constructor, copy assignment & destructor
class String {
    char *buf; int len;
public:
    String(const char *s = "") : len(strlen(s)) {
        buf = new char[len + 1]; strcpy(buf, s);
    }
    // Deep Copy Constructor (called on: String b = a; pass-by-value; return-by-value)
    String(const String &o) : len(o.len) {
        buf = new char[len + 1]; strcpy(buf, o.buf);
    }
    // Copy Assignment Operator
    String& operator=(const String &o) {
        if (this != &o) {
            delete[] buf; len = o.len;
            buf = new char[len + 1]; strcpy(buf, o.buf);
        }
        return *this;
    }
    ~String() { delete[] buf; }
};
Where: Default shallow copy copies only the pointer address, causing double-free crash when destructors run!
Use: Copy constructor parameter MUST be pass-by-reference (const T &o), otherwise passing by value calls the copy constructor infinitely.
Operator overloading: member vs friend (<<, int + Obj, pre/post ++)
class Complex {
    double r, i;
public:
    Complex(double r=0, double i=0) : r(r), i(i) {}
    Complex operator+(const Complex &o) const { return Complex(r + o.r, i + o.i); }
    Complex& operator++()    { ++r; return *this; }                         // prefix ++c
    Complex  operator++(int) { Complex tmp(*this); ++r; return tmp; }       // postfix c++
    friend Complex operator+(double k, const Complex &c) { return Complex(k + c.r, c.i); }
    friend ostream& operator<<(ostream &os, const Complex &c) {
        return os << c.r << " + " << c.i << "i";
    }
};
Where: When the left operand is not of class type (e.g. 5 + obj or cout << obj), the operator MUST be a non-member (friend) function.
Use: Dummy int parameter distinguishes postfix operator++(int) from prefix operator++().
Inheritance, constructor/destructor order, virtual functions & abstract classes
class Shape {
public:
    Shape()  { /* 1. Base ctor runs first */ }
    virtual double area() const = 0; // pure virtual -> Shape is an abstract class
    virtual ~Shape() { /* 4. Base dtor runs last (MUST be virtual!) */ }
};
class Circle : public Shape {
    double r;
public:
    Circle(double r) : Shape(), r(r) { /* 2. Derived ctor runs second */ }
    double area() const override { return 3.14159265 * r * r; }
    ~Circle() override { /* 3. Derived dtor runs first */ }
};
Where: Construction order: Base → Member objects → Derived. Destruction order: exact reverse (Derived → Members → Base).
Use: Always declare the base class destructor virtual when deleting a derived object through a base pointer (Shape *p = new Circle(5); delete p;).
C++ extras: I/O, static & const members, templates, exceptions, namespaces, STLFreq: 4/50/2
Static members, const member functions, function & class templates
template <typename T>
T myMax(T a, T b) { return (a > b) ? a : b; }

template <typename T, int N>
class Stack {
    T arr[N]; int top = 0;
public:
    void push(const T &v) { arr[top++] = v; }
    T pop() { return arr[--top]; }
};
Where: A static data member is shared by all objects of the class and must be defined outside the class (int Counter::count = 0;).
Use: A static member function has no this pointer and can only access static members.
Exception handling (try / throw / catch) & STL vector / map / sort
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
try {
    if (denom == 0) throw runtime_error("Divide by zero");
} catch (const exception &e) {
    cout << e.what() << endl;
}
vector<int> v = {4, 1, 3, 2};
sort(v.begin(), v.end(), [](int a, int b) { return a > b; }); // descending
Where: catch(...) catches any exception type; catch by const reference avoids object slicing.
Use: std::vector grows dynamically (push_back, size, v[i]); std::sort runs in O(N log N).

Trigonometric & hyperbolic identities
$$\begin{aligned}&\sin^2x=\frac{1-\cos 2x}{2},\qquad \cos^2x=\frac{1+\cos 2x}{2},\qquad \cosh^2x-\sinh^2x=1\\&2\sin A\cos B=\sin(A+B)+\sin(A-B),\qquad 2\cos A\cos B=\cos(A+B)+\cos(A-B)\\&2\sin A\sin B=\cos(A-B)-\cos(A+B)\end{aligned}$$
Where: cosh x = ½(e^x + e^{−x}), sinh x = ½(e^x − e^{−x}).

DC circuit laws, analysis methods & network theoremsFreq: 5/50/7
Kirchhoff's Current & Voltage Laws (KCL & KVL) LAW

Kirchhoff's Current Law (KCL — Conservation of Charge): The algebraic sum of all currents entering (or leaving) any node or closed Gaussian surface at any instant is zero.
Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL — Conservation of Energy): The algebraic sum of all branch voltages around any closed loop (mesh) at any instant is zero.

$$\sum_{k=1}^{N} i_k(t) = 0 \quad(\text{at any node}), \qquad \sum_{m=1}^{M} v_m(t) = 0 \quad(\text{around any closed loop})$$
Conditions: Lumped-parameter circuit (circuit dimensions $\ll$ operating wavelength $\lambda$); passive sign convention ($p = +vi$ when current enters the $+$ voltage terminal).
Exam Application: Use KCL at non-reference nodes (Nodal Analysis) and KVL around independent meshes (Mesh Analysis). Tested in 2014–15 Q.1b, 2020–21 Q.2b, 2021–22 Q.5b, 2022–23 Q.5a.
Proof & derivation steps
  1. KCL follows from conservation of charge $q$: since a node cannot store net charge, $\sum i_k = dq_{\text{node}}/dt = 0$.
  2. KVL follows from electrostatic potential energy conservation: moving a test charge $dq$ around a closed path requires net work $\oint \mathbf{E}\cdot d\mathbf{l} = 0 \implies \sum v_k = 0$.
Superposition Theorem THEOREM

Linear Circuit: A circuit composed entirely of linear elements (satisfying homogeneity $f(kx)=kf(x)$ and additivity $f(x_1+x_2)=f(x_1)+f(x_2)$) and linear sources.
Superposition Theorem: In any linear bilateral network containing multiple independent sources, the voltage across or current through any branch equals the algebraic sum of the individual responses caused by each independent source acting alone, with all other independent voltage sources replaced by short circuits ($V=0$) and all other independent current sources replaced by open circuits ($I=0$).

$$v(t) = \sum_{k=1}^{M} v_k(t),\qquad i(t) = \sum_{k=1}^{M} i_k(t);\qquad P = i^2 R = \Big(\sum_{k=1}^M i_k\Big)^2 R \neq \sum_{k=1}^{M} P_k$$
Conditions: Network must be linear; dependent (controlled) sources must NEVER be deactivated—they remain active in every sub-circuit.
Exam Application: Directly applicable to voltage and current, NOT power (since $P = i^2 R$ is non-linear), unless sources operate at different frequencies in steady-state AC.
Proof & derivation steps
  1. Select one independent source; deactivate all other independent sources (short $V$-sources, open $I$-sources). Never deactivate dependent sources.
  2. Solve for the desired branch response $v_k$ or $i_k$ in each sub-circuit.
  3. Sum algebraically: $v = \sum v_k$, $i = \sum i_k$. Compute total power only after summing total current or voltage: $P = (\sum i_k)^2 R \neq \sum i_k^2 R$.
Thévenin's & Norton's Theorems THEOREM

Thévenin's Theorem: Any linear two-terminal network can be replaced at terminals $a$–$b$ by an equivalent voltage source $V_{th} = V_{oc}$ in series with an equivalent resistance $R_{th}$ (or impedance $Z_{th}$).
Norton's Theorem: The same network can be replaced by an equivalent current source $I_N = I_{sc}$ in parallel with $R_N = R_{th}$.

$$V_{th} = V_{oc},\qquad I_N = I_{sc},\qquad R_{th} = R_N = \frac{V_{oc}}{I_{sc}} = \left.\frac{v_{\text{test}}}{i_{\text{test}}}\right|_{\text{indep. sources}=0}$$
Conditions: The external load across $a$–$b$ may be linear or non-linear, but the network being replaced must be linear and have no magnetic/controlled coupling to the external load.
Exam Application: If the circuit contains only dependent sources ($V_{oc}=0, I_{sc}=0$), apply a $1\text{ V}$ or $1\text{ A}$ test source at $a$–$b$ to find $R_{th} = v_{\text{test}}/i_{\text{test}}$ (note $R_{th}$ can be negative when dependent sources supply power, as in BUET 2021–22 Q.3a).
Proof & derivation steps
  1. By linearity of the two-terminal network, terminal voltage $V$ and terminal current $I$ (leaving terminal $a$) satisfy a linear relation $V = A - B I$.
  2. Open-circuit condition ($I = 0$) gives $A = V_{oc} = V_{th}$.
  3. Deactivating independent sources sets $V_{oc} = 0$, leaving $V = -B I$, so $B = R_{th}$. Setting $V = 0$ (short circuit) gives $I_{sc} = V_{th}/R_{th} = I_N$.
Maximum Power Transfer Theorem (DC & AC) THEOREM

DC Case: A resistive load $R_L$ connected to a DC network receives maximum power when $R_L = R_{th}$ (for $R_{th}>0$).
AC Case (Complex Load): In sinusoidal steady state, a complex load $Z_L = R_L + jX_L$ receives maximum average power when $Z_L = Z_{th}^* = R_{th} - jX_{th}$ (complex conjugate matching).
AC Case (Purely Resistive Load): If $X_L = 0$ is fixed, maximum power occurs when $R_L = |Z_{th}| = \sqrt{R_{th}^2 + X_{th}^2}$.

$$R_L = R_{th} \implies P_{\max,\text{DC}} = \frac{V_{th}^2}{4R_{th}};\qquad Z_L = Z_{th}^* \implies P_{\max,\text{AC}} = \frac{|V_{th,\text{rms}}|^2}{4R_{th}} = \frac{|V_{th,\text{peak}}|^2}{8R_{th}}$$
Conditions: Source network $(V_{th}, R_{th})$ is fixed and $R_L$ is the variable parameter ($R_{th} > 0$). At maximum power transfer, load voltage is $V_L = V_{th}/2$ and efficiency is $\eta = 50\%$.
Exam Application: In BUET exams (e.g. 2015–16 Q.2c, 2021–22 Q.8a), always check whether phasor sources are given in peak amplitude $V_m$ (use $|V_{th}|^2 / 8R_{th}$) or RMS (use $|V_{th,\text{rms}}|^2 / 4R_{th}$).
Proof & derivation steps
  1. Write load power: $P_L = I^2 R_L = \dfrac{V_{th}^2 R_L}{(R_{th} + R_L)^2}$.
  2. Differentiate with respect to $R_L$: $\dfrac{dP_L}{dR_L} = V_{th}^2 \dfrac{(R_{th}+R_L)^2 - 2R_L(R_{th}+R_L)}{(R_{th}+R_L)^4} = V_{th}^2 \dfrac{R_{th}-R_L}{(R_{th}+R_L)^3} = 0 \implies R_L = R_{th}$.
  3. Verify $d^2P_L/dR_L^2 |_{R_L=R_{th}} = -V_{th}^2 / (8R_{th}^4) < 0$, confirming a maximum.
